title: Organ-transplant harvesting of HBM from retired accelerators
idea: Like organ donation, debond HBM stacks from end-of-life GPUs below 300 C, using local laser reflow and a solvent-swellable underfill. Retest and re-bump them, then transplant them into low-cost organic-substrate inference cards.
why: Millions of HBM stacks retire with 3-5 year-old accelerators. Reusing even 30% adds supply with no new wafer capacity.

title: Phase-gradient metasurfaces: printed reflectarrays steer wireless memory links inside servers
idea: Roll-print copper patch metasurfaces with fixed phase gradients on films lining chassis walls, redirecting 60-140 GHz beams between memory boards and processors so wireless links get high-gain non-line-of-sight paths.
why: Memory expansion and pooling without cables or backplanes; costs cents per square meter; each chassis layout needs its own pattern.

title: Cable-TV frequency division: many DRAM dies share one RF line
idea: Adapted from DOCSIS cable-TV plant: each DRAM die on a stack or interposer gets its own RF carrier (e.g., eight carriers spread over 10-80 GHz) on one shared transmission line, using tiny on-die mixers instead of dedicated wires. Dies tune in and out like set-top boxes on a multi-drop coax-like trace.
why: Attacks interposer/TSV wiring tax and data movement (facts 5, 6): ~4-8x fewer wires per GB/s and more dies per channel for capacity, targeting <1 pJ/bit at short reach.

title: Laser-drilled TSVs with a single backside landing mask
idea: Po: holes are drilled by light, not printed. Ultrafast lasers drill TSVs maskless through thinned DRAM after front-end and wiring are done, and the only added mask patterns the backside landing pads.
why: Removes the TSV litho, deep etch and their masks from the DRAM flow, easing the HBM TSV tax with lower capital.

title: Two-threshold sensing exports erasure flags over a side channel
idea: Shift from binary to graded certainty at the cell-to-wire boundary: sense amps resolve twice with offset references, marking gray-zone cells as erasures, and a sparse erasure bitmap travels beside the data. Erasure decoding corrects ~2x more than blind errors, so a 1% raw BER needs only ~8% parity.
why: Halves ECC overhead for 1%-BER cells, preserving density while enabling lower VARY (fact 10).

title: Flip the interposer: wafer-scale DRAM becomes the substrate
idea: Reverse the substrate role: instead of a passive silicon interposer carrying GPU and HBM side by side, a full 300 mm DRAM wafer (cell arrays plus a top hybrid-bond layer) is the substrate, and compute chiplets are hybrid-bonded face-down onto it at ~9 um pitch so each chiplet sits directly over its own memory tiles. Global chiplet-to-chiplet wiring runs in the DRAM wafer's upper metals.
why: Removes the passive interposer and HBM TSV stacks (facts 5, 6): micrometre vertical paths at ~0.05-0.1 pJ/bit vs 3-4 pJ/bit for HBM, and ~3x less wafer area per bit than HBM because there are no TSV keep-outs; tile-level redundancy absorbs wafer defects.

title: Delta-merge-on-read lets thousands of fine-tunes share one base
idea: A fine-tuned model differs from its base by a low-rank delta under 1% of parameters. A delta-merge unit in the memory base die applies each tenant's LoRA or sparse delta as base weights stream out, so 100+ tenants each appear to own a full model while memory holds one base plus tiny deltas.
why: Memory per served model ~100x lower; trades a few % quality versus full fine-tunes and adds base-die compute.

title: Stress-metal microsprings for socketed, re-testable HBM
idea: Po: the bumps are springs. A single mask patterns stress-graded MoCr fingers on the DRAM pad field; a release etch lets them curl up into microsprings that press-contact the interposer, so stacks can be tested at speed and swapped before final lock-down.
why: Fixes the known-good-stack problem: bad stacks are caught and replaced instead of scrapping a whole package; 10-20% package yield gain.

title: Railroad standard gauge: open memory-brick footprint any fab can supply
idea: Railroads boomed once gauge was standard: define an open, royalty-free 'memory brick' footprint (bump map, PHY, thermal envelope, test hooks) so DRAM dies from any fab, including U.S. mature-node lines, drop onto any vendor's interposer the way containers fit any ship.
why: Raises usable supply by breaking HBM's three-vendor lock-in and qualification lag: second-source memory chiplets could add capacity within 18-24 months, not 3-5 years.

title: Video-codec P-frames for tensors: ship only deltas between tiles
idea: Adapted from MPEG motion-compensated inter-frame coding: the controller and a logic layer in the DRAM base die keep a reference tile and send only quantized residuals for activation, KV or optimizer tiles that change little step to step. Periodic 'I-frames' bound drift.
why: Data-movement energy and bandwidth (fact 5): temporally correlated AI tensors could need 2-4x fewer bits on the bus, multiplying effective HBM bandwidth and capacity.

title: Spheroidality: radial server board with memory cards as equal spokes
idea: TRIZ #14 Spheroidality: lay out a round motherboard with the CPU or accelerator at the center and memory cards plugged in radially like spokes. Every channel gets the same short trace length, so more DIMMs fit per channel at full speed. Built with existing PCB and connector lines. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Capacity per socket and signal integrity (fact 5): ~1.5-2x more DIMMs per socket at DDR5 speed (2 DIMMs per channel without derating), using cheap commodity DIMMs.

title: Copper wires ultrasonically embedded in thermoplastic form the interposer
idea: Box: LPDDR or HBM-lite x standard x standard x wire-scribed routing x hot-embossed thermoplastic carrier x ultrasonic embedding of 15 um insulated Cu wire. A CNC head lays and embeds insulated wires into the polymer like a multiwire board, with laser-ablated ends forming pads: no etch, no plating, no rinse.
why: Water: substrate fabrication is packaging's main water user; wire scribing is dry, >10x less, and yields an ultra-cheap carrier for memory-dense packages.

title: Uncut wafer-scale DRAM plane with stitched redundancy routing
idea: Wafer-scale engines built for national labs never dice. Leave a DRAM wafer whole, add a stitched cross-reticle RDL mesh, laser-fuse out bad dies and route around them, then face-bond it to a wafer of logic tiles or use it as a 1-2 TB memory board with on-wafer wiring.
why: Removes dicing, per-die packaging and handling (~15-25% of back-end cost) and gives terabyte-scale memory over on-wafer links at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit instead of board traces.

title: Photoconductivity: printed photoconductor pads receive a flood-lit optical reference clock
idea: Flood a whole memory board with a 100-500 MHz modulated light reference from one source through a printed light-guide film; printed photoconductor pads at each memory chip pick it up as a low-jitter reference for local PLLs, removing board clock trees and buffers.
why: I/O energy (fact 5): removes clock distribution power and skew margin; printed parts cost cents; photoconductor speed limits it to reference rates.

title: U.S. hybrid-bond HBM assembly from imported known-good DRAM wafers
idea: Shift the U.S. entry point from the 5-year fab scale to the 18-month packaging scale: tariff-exempt imports of tested DRAM wafers feed U.S.-built hybrid-bonding and stacking lines backed by investment tax credits, producing HBM and DRAM-on-logic domestically; front-end fabs follow once demand is captive.
why: Raises U.S. manufacturability fast (U.S. makes 1-2% of DRAM): packaging lines cost ~$1-2B vs $15B+ fabs and capture ~30-40% of HBM value.

title: Jazz musician plays by ear: self-timed delay-insensitive memory link
idea: A jazz band follows the music, not a metronome: replace the clocked, trained HBM/LPDDR interface with a quasi-delay-insensitive encoding (1-of-4 with acknowledge) whose timing is correct at any temperature, voltage or ageing state, so no retraining is ever needed.
why: Removes timing margin wasted on worst-case 125 C and end-of-life drift, about 20-30% of the link's cycle budget, and skips periodic recalibration stalls over 10 years.

title: Progressive-precision bit-plane streaming of tensors
idea: Worsen: always send all 16 bits of every weight even when the low bits barely matter. Flip: store tensors transposed into bit planes and stream MSB planes first; the accelerator ends the transfer per tile once its error budget is met, so low-order planes move only when needed.
why: Data-movement energy and effective bandwidth: 1.5-3x fewer bits fetched for error-tolerant inference and training tensors; cold low-order planes can live in cheaper memory.

title: Periodic action: follow-the-sun scheduling of memory-heavy jobs
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: memory sits idle on a daily cycle. A global scheduler moves memory-hungry batch jobs (fine-tuning, embedding builds, KV-heavy batch inference) to regions during their off-peak hours and leases out idle DRAM pools through CXL-attached capacity APIs. (No new fab: only existing trailing-node capacity.)
why: Usable supply: 15-25% more useful DRAM-hours from the installed base without any new chips.

title: IRAM fixed: leading-edge logic hybrid-bonded under every DRAM subarray
idea: Berkeley IRAM, Venray TOMI and UPMEM stalled because logic built in a DRAM process is 3-10x slower and wire-starved (about 3 metal layers). Wafer-to-wafer hybrid-bond (<1 um pitch) a 5 nm logic wafer face-to-face to a DRAM array wafer stripped of most periphery, so each 512-row subarray gets its own decoders, sense-adjacent SIMD lane and controller in fast CMOS directly beneath it.
why: Periphery at 49% of the die (fact 7) moves to the logic wafer, giving ~1.6-1.8x more cells per DRAM wafer; near-memory compute at ~0.1 pJ/bit with 10-100x the external bandwidth.

title: Elastomeric zebra sheets make tall stacks solderless and rebuildable
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Stack 32-64 thinned dies interleaved with 30 um anisotropic conductive elastomer sheets (aligned metal filaments in silicone, as in LCD zebra connectors) under a clamped lid; a failed die is swapped by unclamping instead of scrapping the stack.
why: Tall-stack yield is multiplicative (fact 6); rework keeps stack yield near die yield, so 10x tiers cost ~10x dies with no yield penalty and no bonder capex.

title: Cochlear tonotopic wires: passive frequency-split multichannel interposer lines
idea: Each interposer wire carries 4-8 data streams on different RF carriers. At the receiver, a tapered passive resonant 'basilar membrane' transmission line separates the carriers by position, as the cochlea maps pitch to place, so fewer bumps and wires carry the same bandwidth.
why: HBM bump count and shoreline (fact 6): 4-8x bits per wire, so a 1024-2048-wire HBM interface could shrink to ~256 wires, or bandwidth rises at fixed wiring.

title: Multi-carrier RF signaling stacks channels on each interposer wire
idea: Worsen: let each interposer wire carry one baseband NRZ stream, so bandwidth is bump-limited. Flip: modulate 3-4 mm-wave carriers (20-80 GHz) plus baseband onto each low-loss transmission line with on-die filters, multiplying bandwidth per wire without adding bumps or TSVs.
why: HBM TSV tax and periphery (facts 6, 7): 3-4x bandwidth per bump, so fewer TSVs or narrower stacks deliver the same bandwidth.

title: Spin Hall oscillators: frequency-multiplexed carriers put eight channels per interposer wire
idea: Pt/NiFe spin-Hall nano-oscillators, each <1 um^2 and current-tunable from 5-25 GHz, act as tiny carriers; eight differently tuned oscillators share one interposer line and spin-diode detectors demultiplex them at the memory die.
why: Interposer wire density and beachfront (facts 5, 6): 8x fewer wires per unit bandwidth, smaller interposer; nW output power and phase noise are the risks.

title: Reduce-on-the-wire: interposer repeaters sum partial results in flight
idea: Worsen: write every partial sum to memory and read it back at each all-reduce step. Flip: put small adder-repeaters at segment boundaries of long active-bridge wires so gradients and partial dot products accumulate as they travel between chiplets, and only the final sum is written to memory.
why: Data movement: all-reduce memory traffic cut by ~N contributors, shrinking HBM bandwidth and gradient-buffer capacity needs.

title: Magnetorheological chained-particle z-axis film for alignment-free bonds
idea: Mix nickel-cored silver particles into an adhesive film and cure it under a vertical magnetic field, so particles chain into 1-2 um pitch conductive columns. Any pad lands on several columns, so no precision alignment is needed.
why: Lowers die-to-die bonding cost and boosts yield at near-hybrid-bond density, which helps cheap memory stacking.

title: Acousto-optics: Bragg-cell beam steering time-shares one optical link across memories
idea: A surface-acoustic-wave acousto-optic deflector on a lithium niobate interposer steers a host's free-space beam among 32 memory chiplets in ~100 ns by changing the RF drive frequency, forming a solid-state switched memory fabric with no electrical crossbar.
why: Data movement and pooling (fact 5): one transceiver serves 32 memory targets, cutting SerDes count and stranded memory; switch time suits page migration, not per-access.

title: RFID backscatter reads: memory reflects bits instead of driving them
idea: Batteryless RFID tags talk by toggling their antenna load to reflect the reader's carrier. The host drives a continuous carrier onto each read lane; the memory base die returns data by switching a tiny termination impedance between reflect and absorb, and the host's coherent receiver demodulates.
why: Memory-side transmit energy drops ~10-50x (a switch toggle instead of a line driver) and stack heat falls, allowing taller stacks; the host carrier is shared across lanes.

title: Hybrid Memory Cube revived: packetized cube over UCIe, no SerDes, no interposer
idea: Micron's HMC died from long-reach SerDes power (~10 pJ/bit total) and latency plus a closed consortium. Keep its smart logic base die and packet protocol, but replace the SerDes with clock-forwarded UCIe-Standard links (~0.5 pJ/bit) over a plain organic substrate at 2-10 mm reach, and publish the packet layer as an open spec so the cube becomes a drop-in memory chiplet that any accelerator can place without CoWoS.
why: HBM interposer/TSV capital and CoWoS scarcity (fact 6) plus link energy (fact 5): ~5x lower link energy than HMC, no silicon interposer, and logic-die features (ECC, repair, refresh scheduling) kept.

title: MRI-safe metal-free stack: optical vias through silicon at 1310 nm
idea: MRI-compatible implants must avoid metal paths. Silicon is transparent above 1.1 um, so give each die in a stack aligned micro-emitter and germanium photodiode arrays and pass data vertically through the dies as light; only power needs vias.
why: Removes signal TSVs and their capacitance; sub-100 fJ/bit vertical links (~10x below TSV+PHY paths), looser die alignment, and less TSV area tax.

title: Resonant adiabatic memory bus recycles wire charge via LC tank
idea: Combine resonant clocking's on-chip LC tank with the wide data bus: interposer/HBM data lines become part of a resonant network where transitioning lines swing sinusoidally through an inductor and hand their CV2 energy back to the tank instead of dumping it to ground; steady bits park.
why: Data movement and the voltage floor: recovers ~50-70% of bus switching energy at interposer lengths without lowering voltage.

title: Wireless-charger resonance recycles memory-bus switching energy
idea: Adapted from resonant inductive phone chargers: a wide HBM-style bus is driven as part of an LC tank with on-interposer spiral inductors. Line capacitance charges and discharges sinusoidally, and most of the CV^2 energy returns to the tank instead of being burned in drivers.
why: CV^2 floor and data movement (facts 5, 10): resonant drive can recover 50-80% of switching energy on wide, clock-like buses.

title: Adiabatic resonant links that recycle wire charge every cycle
idea: Reverse dissipate-and-replace signalling: each interposer line's capacitance forms an LC tank with an on-die spiral or package inductor, and data is encoded by phase or selective clamping of the resonant swing, so most of the CV^2 energy sloshes back instead of burning in drivers.
why: CV^2 floor and data-movement energy (facts 5, 10): 3-5x lower energy on long interposer and substrate lines (~0.5 vs ~2 pJ/bit), at the cost of fixed-frequency operation.

title: Periodic action: resonant LC-tank data bus recycling switching energy
idea: TRIZ #19 Periodic action: make each wide-bus line part of an LC tank with an inductor in the interposer, so the line rings sinusoidally at the clock rate and data is encoded by conditional phase injection. Energy swings between L and C instead of being dumped on every toggle.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and voltage floor (fact 10): 3-5x lower IO energy on capacitive 1-2k-bit buses.

title: Mercury delay-line revival: recirculating photonic loop broadcasts streaming weights
idea: Replace the 1940s mercury tank with a ~2 m low-loss silicon-nitride spiral on the interposer (~10 ns, 64 wavelengths x 50 Gb/s) closed by an SOA regenerator; a weight tile read once from HBM recirculates for N laps and 8-16 compute chiplets tap it each lap via ring drop filters.
why: Facts 5/8: each weight byte crosses the HBM PHY once instead of once per consumer or per micro-batch step, cutting DRAM reads and pJ/bit on broadcast/expert-shared traffic ~4-8x; loop holds only ~32 kbit so it is a broadcast medium with temporal reuse, not a store.

title: Resonant LC adiabatic signaling on interposer memory wires
idea: First principles: abrupt switching burns CV^2/2 per transition no matter the driver, but adiabatic charging over time T burns only (RC/T)*CV^2. Pattern thin-film spiral inductors in the interposer RDL so each HBM lane group forms an LC tank with its own wire capacitance, ringing at the bus rate; data selects which wires join the resonant phase, and their charge returns to the tank instead of to ground.
why: Attacks data-movement energy (fact 5): with RC/T~0.05 on a 5 mm interposer wire, link energy could fall from ~3-4 pJ/bit toward ~0.3-0.5 pJ/bit (5-10x).

title: Resonant LC tank bus recycles CV2 energy every clock cycle
idea: Match the bus to a resonant timescale: inductors integrated in the interposer let the wide bus's wire capacitance swing inside an LC tank, with data encoded on an adiabatic sinusoidal clock-power line. Charge sloshes back between L and C each cycle instead of being dumped to ground.
why: Breaks the CV2 floor on interface energy (facts 5, 10): ~50-70% lower energy for wide parallel memory buses.

title: Reclaimed server DIMMs reborn as CXL memory pools
idea: Substitute new DRAM purchases with DDR4/DDR5 DIMMs pulled from decommissioned servers: a small team builds an FPGA or off-the-shelf CXL-controller card holding 8-16 used DIMMs, screens them with an on-card pattern tester, and sells them as CXL Type-3 capacity tiers.
why: Cost per bit and scarcity: reused bits cost ~10-20% of new ones and add supply with zero fab capex during the 4x price spike.

title: Porous-silicon release layers recycle donor wafers across forty tiers
idea: Forced: 10x density at the same cost. Build DRAM on a porous-silicon cleave layer (ELTRAN-style), transfer only the 2 um device film into the stack, then re-epi and reuse the donor substrate 10-20 times; 40+ films fit in the height of three normal dies.
why: Silicon and quartz-crucible chokepoint plus wafer cost: substrate cost per tier falls ~90%, paying for the extra tiers, so ~10x bits per footprint at similar package cost.

title: Single-wire earth-return revival: bulk silicon as shared stack return path
idea: Revive the telegraph's single-wire earth return: use the heavily doped bulk of ohmically bonded dies as the common signal and power return, so the stack needs signal vias only, not paired ground vias.
why: Constraint: halving vertical via count halves the slower fluorine-free (HBr/laser) via process time, making it economic; shrinks the HBM TSV area tax (fact 6) ~30-40%, with substrate noise the main risk.

title: OSP finishes failed after reflows; graphene/h-BN monolayers replace ENEPIG gold
idea: Organic solderability preservatives were the cheap alternative to Ni/Pd/Au (ENEPIG) pad finishes but failed because they degrade after multiple reflows, which multi-die memory packages need. Coat Cu substrate pads with a transferred or low-temperature plasma-grown monolayer of graphene or h-BN that blocks oxidation through repeated 260 C cycles yet is thin enough for Cu-Cu or Zn-Al joints to break through during bonding.
why: Removes Pd and Au from every memory package substrate pad, cutting BOM and precious-metal supply risk; C, B and N only.

title: Mirror lid reflects free-space light between memory and logic
idea: Box: DRAM chiplet x standard x photodiode array x upward-facing microLED arrays bounced off a molded aspheric mirror lid x dry-laminated power-only carrier x injection molding. Chiplets need only a few power layers below; all memory data travels as light up to the lid and back down to the processor.
why: Water: removes the interposer and high-layer-count signal substrate (the wet-heavy parts), ~10x less water; bandwidth no longer tied to shoreline.

title: Photonic phase-change memory read by light without conversion
idea: Eliminate O/E/O conversion at disaggregated memory: store bits in GST or Sb2Se3 patches on silicon-nitride waveguides whose phase state sets transmission, and read them with WDM light pulses arriving directly from compute.
why: Read is just attenuation with no modulator or photodiode at the memory, cutting link-plus-access energy toward ~1 pJ/bit; ~1e8-1e12 endurance limits it to read-mostly data.

title: Coolant that is also the power supply: in-stack redox microchannels
idea: Combine interlayer microfluidic cooling with a redox flow battery: a vanadium or organic electrolyte pumped through microchannels between HBM dies passes porous electrodes on each die, generating ~1 V locally while carrying away heat, so most power TSVs and bumps are replaced by fluid.
why: HBM TSV tax and thermal ceiling: power/ground TSVs are roughly half the via count; replacing them frees ~30-50% of TSVs and lets stacks grow past today's thermal limit.

title: Anti-weight: microfluidic cooling interlayer lifting heat between compute and DRAM
idea: TRIZ #8 Anti-weight (counter a harmful load with a force from the environment): put a 100 um silicon interlayer between a hot accelerator and the DRAM stacked on it. The interlayer has through-vias and two-phase dielectric coolant microchannels that carry compute heat sideways, keeping the DRAM below 85 C.
why: Data movement (fact 5) and refresh (fact 3): memory-on-logic stacking (~10x lower pJ/bit than HBM) becomes possible without the 2x refresh rate required above 85 C.

title: Lost-wax cast microfluidic cooling around taller memory stacks
idea: Print sacrificial polycarbonate lines around and between HBM stacks, mold over them, then burn them out like investment casting so coolant channels remain inside the encapsulant.
why: Heat limits stack height; in-package cooling enables 16-24-high stacks, raising density per footprint.

title: Single vacuum cluster: plasma-dice, CO2-snow clean, activate, bond
idea: Box: HBM DRAM x standard x standard x die-to-wafer hybrid bond x Si x integrated vacuum cluster with plasma dicing, CO2-snow particle removal and plasma activation. Wafers enter once and leave as bonded stacks; dies never touch water or room air, so no pre-bond DI clean is needed.
why: Water: removes dicing water, megasonic cleans and rinses (>10x); particle-free surfaces also raise hybrid-bond yield against the HBM yield loss (fact 6).

title: Radio-telescope corner-turn base die gives free transposes
idea: Radio correlators (SKA, ALMA) spend much of their memory budget on the 'corner turn' that transposes time-major data to frequency-major. Store tiles diagonally skewed across banks and add a butterfly transpose network in the HBM base die, so a matrix written row-major streams out column-major at full burst efficiency.
why: Strided/transposed reads waste 50-90% of fetched bytes (page overfetch); attention, FFT and weight-gradient transposes run at full efficiency, ~2-5x effective bandwidth in those phases.

title: Wireless in-package multicast of shared weights to many GPUs
idea: Po: memory that shouts instead of whispers. One weights-holding DRAM stack drives a 140 GHz antenna into the metal package lid cavity, which acts as a shared waveguide, so all eight accelerators in the package receive the same weight stream at once instead of each storing its own copy.
why: Model weights are replicated per GPU; de-duplication frees 30-60% of HBM capacity for KV cache, and one transmission serving N readers cuts energy per reader-bit ~N-fold.

title: Harvest-and-restack business for failed HBM stacks
idea: Substitute scrapping whole 12/16-high stacks that fail final test with a laser lift-off service: stacks are built with a thin absorbing debond layer at each tier, failed dies are released by a laser through the stack edge, and good dies are re-bonded into new stacks.
why: Fact 6 yield loss of 20-30%: recover most of the known-good dies in failed stacks, adding ~10-20% effective HBM supply.

title: Solar bypass-diode die skipping to ship stacks with dead tiers
idea: Bypass diodes keep a shaded solar string producing. In the same way, each core die carries anti-fuse-programmed bypass switches on its TSV pass-through paths. A die that fails after stacking is skipped electrically, and the stack ships as a lower-capacity SKU (for example 11-high) instead of being scrapped.
why: HBM loses 20-30% yield at stacking. Turning scrap into binned capacity could bring back most of that, about 15-25% more sellable bits per wafer start.

title: 1950s ferroelectric matrix switches remap failed HBM dies after bonding
idea: Revive Bell Labs' 1952 BaTiO3 ferroelectric matrix as HZO ferroelectric-FET crosspoint switches in the HBM base die that nonvolatilely reroute channels and TSV groups around a dead core die or bad TSV cluster after stacking, holding state with zero power.
why: Fact 6: much of HBM's 20-30% yield loss arises at stack/bond level; post-bond repair could recover roughly half of it (~10-15% more sellable stacks per wafer start) with negligible area.

title: Re-meltable laser-reflow microbumps make memory stacks repairable
idea: Worsen: bond permanently so one die failing after stacking kills the whole stack and its host GPU. Flip: join dies with encapsulated In-Sn-Bi microbumps that stay solid in operation (<105 C) but re-melt near 140 C, and use layer-selective laser reflow to lift and replace a failed die after stack test.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): converts compounding stack scrap into a rework step; reclaims good dies and the GPU, ~10-20% more good stacks.

title: Ion migration: electroformed silver filaments grow and repair vias after stacking
idea: Bond dies through a thin chalcogenide solid-electrolyte layer between coarsely aligned pads; a post-bond forming pulse drives Ag+ ions to grow filaments bridging whichever pads face each other, and any open or degraded bond found in field test is re-grown by another pulse.
why: HBM yield loss of 20-30% (fact 6): turns opens into repairable defects and relaxes alignment to a few um; filament current capacity and long-term stability are the risks.

title: Hf: HfO2 antifuse farms enable massive post-stack HBM repair
idea: Add a dense HfO2-breakdown antifuse array (1T1AF, ~0.1 um2 each) to the HBM base die that remaps failing core-die rows, columns and whole sub-banks found after stacking and at-speed test, far beyond today's limited post-package repair fuses.
why: HBM yield (fact 6): defects discovered after bonding are the main 20-30% loss; 10-100x more repair elements could recover a large share with zero host change.

title: N-plus-one HBM: a spare die rewired in after stacking
idea: Ideal: stacking never wastes a good die. Closest achievable: build 13-high stacks sold as 12-high, with a crossbar of redundant TSV lanes in the base die so any one failing core die or TSV column is mapped out at final test.
why: Fact 6: converts 20-30% stack yield loss into a fixed ~8% capacity overhead; stack yield rises toward 90%+, cutting HBM cost per good bit ~15-20%.

title: Universal pre-built interposer customised by a single via mask
idea: Po: every package uses the same package. Pre-fabricate a standard interposer with a dense crossbar of horizontal and vertical lines in volume, and personalise each product with only one via mask that connects chosen crossings.
why: Amortises interposer masks across all products; per-product mask cost and lead time drop ~5x, lowering capital per memory package.

title: Qubit-fridge FDM: dozens of memory channels on one trace
idea: Quantum computers frequency-multiplex qubit readout because fridge wires are precious. Carry 16-32 memory channels as QAM subcarriers on one wideband line with integrated mm-wave mixers at both ends, so a far memory module needs a few lines instead of hundreds of pins.
why: Cuts pin, beachfront and routing cost ~10x for capacity tiers, letting memory sit on cheap remote boards; the trade is mixer power.

title: Laptop panel-self-refresh: mirrored dictionaries deduplicate memory link traffic
idea: Laptop eDP panels self-refresh so the GPU stops resending unchanged frames. Keep synchronized small dictionaries of recent 64 B lines at both ends of the memory link; when a line or near-match is already in the far dictionary, send a 10-bit index plus a sparse diff instead of 512 bits.
why: Repeated lines (zero pages, shared prefixes, embeddings) are common; at 50-90% hit rates link energy per access falls ~3-10x without touching cells.

title: Predictive link sends only surprises, leaving sub-1% residual errors
idea: Shift from sending bits to sending surprises: identical predictors (previous value plus learned delta) run at both ends of the memory link and only mispredicted bits are sent; since consumers already absorb 1% cell errors, the predictor may be lossy and residual mismatches are simply not retransmitted.
why: ~2-4x effective link bandwidth for smooth tensor streams (fact 5), cutting pJ per useful bit proportionally.

title: Charge-sharing pooled reads send sums, not raw bytes
idea: Box: 1T1C x multi-wordline activation x analog charge sharing across N cells digitized by an ADC in the base die x TSV x Si x standard. Activating several cells on one bitline averages their charge into an analog sum the base die digitizes, so pooling, attention accumulation or Bloom-filter reductions ship one value instead of N.
why: Data movement: 4-16x fewer bits across TSVs and package for reduction-heavy AI kernels.

title: Aerodynamic focusing: aerosol-jet printed staircase edge wiring replaces stack TSVs
idea: Stack DRAM dies offset like a staircase and aerosol-jet print conductive traces over printed dielectric ramps down the exposed edges, so every die connects to the base die without a single TSV.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): reclaims TSV area and yield loss and removes via etch/fill tools; lower edge bandwidth suits capacity-optimized (CXL) stacks.

title: Damascus-fold edge wiring: film thickness sets 40 nm pitch
idea: Deposit 100 alternating copper/oxide films 20 nm thick, or fold-laminate metal foil like Damascus steel, then slice the stack on edge and polish it. The face shows parallel wires whose pitch is set by deposition thickness, and this becomes a bridge die between memory and logic.
why: Sub-EUV wire pitch with no lithography at all; claims bridge densities beyond today's silicon bridges for HBM-class links.

title: Nondestructive-read multicast: one row read serves many requesters
idea: Worsen: use destructive reads so every read is written back and each requester triggers its own activation. Flip: with capacitorless nondestructive cells (gain cells, SRAM), let the interface broadcast one row read to all subscribed chiplets via a multicast tag, with no restore phase.
why: Destructive read and overfetch (fact 8): restore energy removed and shared data read once instead of N times, up to Nx bandwidth gain for shared weights.

title: Bell Labs beam-lead revival: cantilevered gold beams tile dies interposer-free
idea: Revive Lepselter's 1960s beam-lead process: gold beams plated on the die are released by a KOH/TMAH back-etch through a laser-ablated hard mask (no HF, no fluorine plasma) to cantilever 50-100 um past the edge, then thermocompression-bonded to neighboring memory and logic dies.
why: Constraint and capital: avoids the silicon interposer's fluorine-based DRIE and the CoWoS bottleneck; 10 um-pitch edge beams give ~100 lanes per mm of die edge, enough for wide memory links at low cost.

title: Kerr soliton microcomb: one shared laser powers all memory chiplet optics
idea: A single SiN Kerr microcomb per rack generates 64-128 phase-locked wavelengths distributed over fiber as an optical power utility; memory chiplets carry only modulators and detectors, no lasers, removing per-chiplet laser cost, heat and failure.
why: Makes optical memory links (fact 5) cheap at DRAM volume; removes lasers from hot memory packages; 64 wavelengths x 32 Gb/s per fiber.

title: Single-metal-layer bridge enabled by mirrored crossing-free ballouts
idea: Po: an interposer with only one wiring layer. Co-design HBM and GPU bump maps as mirror images so every connection routes without crossings, then build the bridge die with just one patterned 1 um copper layer in a mature fab.
why: Cuts bridge or interposer masks from 4-6 to one, slashing 2.5D cost and letting U.S. mature fabs make the parts.

title: Print-on-demand maskless interposers written straight from CAD
idea: Write each interposer's RDL directly with laser direct imaging plus electrohydrodynamic jet printing, so no masks exist, like print-on-demand books. Small-lot memory configurations become economic.
why: Removes mask cost and lead time, so custom memory-compute packages are cheap at low volume, all without EUV.

title: Garden hose: flyover twinax from package straight to memory modules
idea: Like a garden hose run over the lawn instead of under it: memory signals leave the processor package on flyover twinax cables to near-socket CAMM modules, bypassing lossy PCB traces, so DDR5/LPDDR runs faster at lower drive energy. Off-the-shelf cable assemblies.
why: pJ/bit and bandwidth of off-package DRAM: 20-30% less I/O energy and higher speed bins on existing chips.

title: Transferred micron-thin array films replace thinned TSV dies
idea: Ideal: stacking costs no silicon area at all. Closest achievable: instead of thinning HBM dies to 30-50 um and drilling 5-10 um TSVs with keep-out zones, smart-cut a 1-2 um device film of each DRAM array and bond it sequentially, linking tiers with ~0.5 um nano-vias that need almost no keep-out.
why: Fact 6 TSV tax: via plus keep-out area falls from several % of die to <0.5%; stack height shrinks so 24-32 tiers fit the current 720 um envelope, with lower thermal resistance.

title: Telecom MEMS optical cross-connects time-share memory pools among accelerators
idea: Adapted from MEMS-mirror optical circuit switches in telecom cores: fiber links between memory shelves and accelerators are re-pointed in milliseconds, moving terabytes of DRAM to whichever job is in its memory-heavy phase (e.g., decode versus prefill).
why: Raises usable supply by cutting overprovisioning; circuit-switched light adds no per-bit switching energy; ~20-40% less DRAM per cluster.

title: MgB2 flux-loop memory banks linked to processors by fiber
idea: Worsen: store bits as charge that leaks at room temperature. Flip: store bits as a persistent single-flux-quantum current in MgB2 superconducting loops at ~20 K, cooled by closed-cycle cryocoolers rather than liquid helium, and link them to room-temperature processors over fiber with cryogenic photodetectors driving the inputs.
why: Zero leakage, attojoule switching and no refresh; avoids the helium chokepoint by using a 39 K superconductor. Cryocooler wall-plug cost is the risk.

title: MEMS-mirror optical switches rewire memory pools per job
idea: Invert 'memory-to-compute wiring is fixed at build time': use U.S. micromirror fabs (Dallas DLP heritage) to build optical circuit switches that reassign fiber links from memory sleds to accelerators per job within milliseconds.
why: Fixed configurations strand 20-40% of fleet DRAM; reconfigurable pooling raises utilization so fewer bits must be bought.

title: Idle chat sessions keep tokens, not KV caches, until resumed
idea: A KV entry is ~100-500 KB per token but the token that produced it is 2 bytes, and most KV memory belongs to sessions idle between user turns. Evict idle sessions to token IDs only and re-prefill them on return using cheap older-node recompute chiplets, trading FLOPs for bytes.
why: Resident KV memory falls 100x+ for typical chat duty cycles; trades resume latency and prefill energy.

title: Plywood cross-laminated thin-glass interposer fused in one bake
idea: Laser-drill and print orthogonal routing onto 50 um glass sheets, alternating direction like plywood grain, then stack and fuse them at ~600 C into one monolithic interposer. Each sheet is tested before lamination.
why: Mask-free multilayer interposer with glass's low loss and flatness; claims ~3x lower cost than silicon interposers and higher yield from known-good layers.

title: B: turn idle US borosilicate glass lines into interposer fabs
idea: Retool shuttered or underused US display/solar glass finishing lines to produce 510x515 mm borosilicate glass-core panels with laser-drilled through-glass vias for HBM packaging, using the existing US specialty-glass base instead of building new silicon interposer capacity.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital (facts 4, 6): panels give ~5-8x the usable area of a 300 mm interposer wafer at a fraction of capex, breaking the CoWoS-style interposer bottleneck for HBM.

title: Backside power mesh halves HBM through-silicon via count
idea: Box: HBM DRAM x standard x standard x front-side signal-only hybrid bonds plus backside nano-TSV power grid x thinned Si x backside-power flow borrowed from logic. Power and ground, about half of HBM's TSVs, move to a backside metal mesh fed by dense 0.5 um nano-TSVs, so only signal TSVs remain in the keep-out zone.
why: TSV tax (fact 6): ~40-50% fewer large TSVs, ~3-5% die area recovered, and lower IR drop that permits taller stacks.

title: Millimetre-wave backscatter antennas on each DRAM die
idea: Po: the memory answers without speaking. One top-metal mask adds a small antenna per die; the GPU floods the package cavity with a 140 GHz carrier and each die returns read data by switching its antenna load with a single transistor, RFID-style.
why: Near-zero transmit power on the DRAM die and no TSV or bump for read return; strong energy per bit gain for wide broadcast-style reads.

title: Z-RAM revived as a bonded cache tile, sense amps in logic below
idea: Innovative Silicon's capacitorless floating-body Z-RAM died because it required SOI logic wafers and its sense margin collapsed under logic-process variation, so AMD dropped it. Build the floating-body array alone on its own SOI chiplet, with no compromise to the CPU process, and hybrid-bond it over a logic die that holds low-offset, auto-zeroed sense amplifiers and refresh logic for every 64 kb tile at 1-2 um bond pitch.
why: Avoids the capacitor charge wall (fact 1) and the TSV tax: a capacitorless near-memory tier at ~2-3x SRAM density with face-to-face bandwidth that absorbs external DRAM traffic.

title: Printed polymer optical waveguides replace helium-drawn glass fiber links
idea: Combine package build-up layers with optics: photo-pattern siloxane polymer waveguides (LED-cured) into the substrate and board to link co-packaged optical engines on GPUs and memory modules over 10-50 cm. Glass fiber needs helium for preform consolidation and draw cooling; polymer waveguides need none.
why: Optical memory disaggregation at ~1-2 pJ/bit without fiber-attach cost/yield, on a rare-gas-free supply chain.

title: Store tokens, not KV: base-die engines recompute keys and values
idea: Worsen: hold gigabytes of KV cache per long conversation in capacitors. Flip: keep only token IDs (2 bytes per token) plus sparse activation checkpoints, and let matrix engines in the memory base die regenerate K and V for evicted spans on demand, trading cheap FLOPs for scarce bits.
why: Capacity: KV per token (~100 KB+ in large models) collapses to bytes plus checkpoints, 10-100x less memory for long contexts at some recompute energy.

title: Upcycle commodity DRAM dies with pad-rearranging RDL
idea: Rearrange the pads, not the die: buy known-good LPDDR bare dies, and in a university nanofab add a polyimide plus electroplated-Cu redistribution layer (contact aligner, 5 um lines) that fans the edge pad row into an area array matched to a logic test chip, then flip-chip the two face-to-face.
why: U.S. manufacturability and capital: wide-I/O-like short links from commodity dies with ~$1M of tools, showing ~1 pJ/bit without a TSV line (facts 5, 6).

title: Interposers made from reclaimed monitor and reject wafers
idea: Po: fab garbage is the interposer. Collect test, monitor and scratched prime wafers, re-polish them, laser-drill vias with no mask, and add one thick copper redistribution layer with a single mask for simple HBM-to-logic routing.
why: Removes demand for new silicon and crucible-grown wafers in interposers, cutting cost and quartz-crucible exposure.

title: X-Celeprint transfer printing failed in displays; print DRAM dielets onto logic
idea: Micro-transfer printing (X-Celeprint/X Display) stalled because displays needed millions of microLEDs placed at six-sigma yield. Memory needs only tens to hundreds of large dielets per wafer: undercut-release 5-10 um thick DRAM dielets, pick them in parallel with PDMS stamps onto a logic wafer, and connect them with one lithographic Cu/Al redistribution layer over the planarized surface, with no bumps, solder or TSVs.
why: Removes microbump solder (Sn, Ag, In) and TSVs (fact 6), selects known-good dielets, and gives 2-5 um RDL pitch at ~0.1 pJ/bit; Si, O, C, Cu and Al only.

title: TSV-free cube stacking with sidewall-printed interconnect
idea: Ideal: a memory stack with no holes in it. Closest achievable: route each DRAM die's bus to one edge, stack dies like playing cards, polish the stack face and pattern a 2 um redistribution layer across the exposed edges so all vertical wiring lives on the sidewall outside the silicon.
why: Fact 6: eliminates TSV etch, fill and reveal and their share of the 20-30% stack yield loss and area tax; uses planar tools only and lets dies be sorted before assembly.

title: Keyssa's contactless connector failed in phones; it fits gold-free memory modules
idea: Keyssa's 60 GHz near-field 'kiss' connectors failed commercially because phone connectors were cheap and good enough. Server memory slots are now the signal-integrity wall at DDR5-8800+ and use gold-plated contacts, so replace the DIMM edge connector with an array of CMOS 60-140 GHz near-field couplers with plain Cu antennas, giving a sealed, wear-free, hot-swappable module interface.
why: Removes Au contact plating and connector wear failures; contactless lanes at ~1-2 pJ/bit allow faster modules and more slots per channel, raising capacity per socket.

title: Compound-eye infrared links shining straight through stacked dies
idea: Silicon is transparent above ~1.1 um, so each DRAM tier carries tiny bonded 1.3 um emitter and detector pixels under a microlens array, like an insect's ommatidia, that beam data vertically through the thinned dies above and below. Hundreds of vertical optical channels replace signal TSVs with no drilling and no keep-out zones.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): signal TSVs and their keep-out area disappear and vertical bandwidth scales with pixel count; target <0.3 pJ/bit per vertical hop.

title: Co: cobalt-alloy magnetic-core coils replace signal TSVs inside HBM
idea: Inside the stack, couple core dies inductively with on-die coils wrapped around electroplated CoFe/CoZrTa thin-film magnetic cores (relative permeability ~500), boosting coupling through 20-30 um thinned dies so signal paths need no TSVs; the base die still presents the standard HBM PHY.
why: HBM TSV tax (fact 6): removes signal-TSV area, keep-out and TSV yield loss at ~0.1-0.3 pJ/bit; only a few large power TSVs remain.

title: Roof-shingle die stacks with aerosol-jet printed ramp interconnects
idea: Offset each die by 100 um like roof shingles so edge pads stay exposed, then aerosol-jet 3D-print conductive ramps down the staircase to make the vertical bus. No TSVs are drilled into the DRAM.
why: Removes TSV area and stacking yield tax; lets standard commodity dies with edge pads become wide-I/O stacks.

title: E-paper shelf-label stepwise charging of memory buses
idea: Electronic shelf labels last a decade on a coin cell partly by driving lines in small steps from tank capacitors. Charge each long column-datapath and interposer line through a ladder of N tank-capacitor rails; each step dissipates ~1/N of the CV2 and the tanks recapture charge on discharge.
why: With N=8-10 steps line energy falls ~8-10x, at the cost of ~N-times slower edges, which suits wide-slow buses.

title: Dielectric waveguiding: extruded polymer mm-wave tubes carry memory traffic one meter
idea: Continuously extrude low-loss PTFE/PE dielectric waveguide ribbons and launch 140-220 GHz carriers from CMOS transceivers into them, giving 100+ Gb/s per tube over 1 m with no lasers for board-to-board memory-pool links.
why: Data movement (fact 5): cheaper than optics and longer than copper at ~1-2 pJ/bit; enables disaggregated DRAM pools that raise utilization.

title: Yield-elastic stacks binned by good-bank count, not die count
idea: Worsen: scrap a 12-high stack because one die has a bad bank, compounding loss with height. Flip: design the base die to remap at bank granularity across dies and sell stacks by working-bank count (e.g., 12 dies sold as 10.5-die capacity), so partially bad dies go into product instead of scrap.
why: HBM yield loss (fact 6, 20-30%): recovers most stack-level scrap, roughly +15-25% sellable HBM bits from the same wafers.

title: Address-event memory bus transmits only nonzero values as spikes
idea: Combine neuromorphic address-event representation with the DRAM interface: the base die encodes each burst as (index, value) events for nonzero bytes and drives an asynchronous clockless bus that toggles only when an event fires; zero runs cost no transitions and the host rebuilds dense lines.
why: Interface energy and effective bandwidth: quantized ML activations/KV caches are 40-90% zero; 2-5x lower interface energy and higher effective bandwidth on sparse tensors.

title: Downhole drilling engineer: FD-SOI PHY with temperature-tracking back-bias
idea: Oil-well tools run for years at 175 C on SOI: build the memory interface PHY and base logic on FD-SOI and let an on-die temperature loop set the back-gate bias so threshold voltage, leakage and delay stay constant from -40 C to 150 C.
why: Junction leakage disappears with SOI, and back-bias holds timing and I/O power flat at 125 C, so links run at full speed with no hot derating.

title: Ribbon-grown silicon interposer blanks without quartz crucibles
idea: Pull interposer-grade silicon as continuous ribbon through a graphite die (edge-defined film-fed growth) instead of Czochralski boules from Spruce Pine quartz crucibles. Interposers do not need prime crystal quality, and ribbon growth avoids sawing kerf.
why: Cuts reliance on high-purity quartz (>80% one source) and ~40% kerf loss for the large passive silicon used in HBM packaging.

title: Quantize-on-write base die stores KV at 4 bits transparently
idea: Worsen: store every KV value at FP16 although attention tolerates far less. Flip: the HBM base die applies per-block scaled 4-bit quantization with outlier side tables on write and dequantizes on read, so the host still sees FP16 while the array holds ~3.5x more tokens.
why: Usable capacity and bandwidth: ~3-4x more KV per GB and ~3x fewer array bits moved per token.

title: Laser-written waveguides inside glass interposers link HBM optically
idea: Po: wires are written, not printed. Femtosecond lasers write buried 3D waveguides inside a glass interposer that connect edge-coupled micro-ring transmitters on the HBM base die to the GPU, routing hundreds of WDM channels in 3D with zero lithography.
why: Lets HBM sit 5-50 mm away, breaking the GPU shoreline limit (more stacks per GPU) at ~1 pJ/bit and with no interposer masks.
